title: Masters Round 4: What to know about Rory McIlroy’s second win at Augusta National
content:
Augusta National prides itself on history. For the second consecutive April, a man from Northern Ireland authored new chapters in that voluminous book.

Here are the top numbers and notes to know from the final round of the 90th Masters Tournament.

1. A year after becoming just the sixth man in golf’s modern era to complete the career grand slam, Rory McIlroy somehow joined an even shorter list by becoming the fourth to go back-to-back at the Masters. McIlroy joined Jack Nicklaus (1965-66), Nick Faldo (1989-90) and Tiger Woods (2001-02) as the only players in the 90 editions of the tournament to successfully defend their title.

McIlroy took a tournament-record six-shot lead into the weekend but saw his advantage evaporate by the time he got to the 13th tee Saturday. Still, his phenomenal opening 36 holes built enough cushion to make up for any weekend stumbles. With closing rounds of 73 and 71, McIlroy is the first player to win the Masters while losing strokes to the field on the weekend. McIlroy needed 12 more shots over the final two rounds than he did Thursday and Friday. That ties Sam Snead in 1952 for the largest such differential in the last two rounds by a Masters champion.

2. McIlroy flirted with danger for the first two rounds, building his six-stroke lead despite hitting less than half of his fairways. It was fitting, then, that McIlroy’s last drive of the week was wildly off line, stoking one last sequence of championship intrigue. McIlroy hit just 31 fairways for the week, the fewest by a Masters winner in recorded history. The previous mark belonged to Woods in 2005 and Adam Scott in 2013 with 32 apiece.

Despite the miss at 18, McIlroy was much more accurate off the tee Sunday. At one point, he hit eight straight fairways from the fifth through 14th holes. That stretch alone would have equaled his best total in any other round for the tournament. In all, McIlroy was 5-under-par this week when missing the fairway on a par 4 or par 5. Since 2000, the only player with a better score to par when doing that in a Masters win was Hideki Matsuyama in 2021.

3. McIlroy’s sixth major championship puts him one shy of Harry Vardon for the most in men’s professional golf history by a player from Europe. He also is the only player in the men’s game younger than 50 with six or more career major wins. Other legends with exactly six major titles include Lee Trevino, Phil Mickelson and Faldo.

McIlroy got his second Masters win in his 18th career start at Augusta. Only one player in history has won his second Masters victory later in his career in terms of attempts. Ben Crenshaw won his second Masters title in 1994 — his 24th career appearance. Winning back-to-back in any major championship is rare, but it’s especially unique to do it with as many previous starts at an event before doing it. Before McIlroy won in his 17th and 18th Masters starts, the longest such wait was 11th and 12th — by Padraig Harrington, Woods and James Braid, each at The Open Championship.

4. Scottie Scheffler entered the weekend 12 shots back, looking to mount the largest 36-hole comeback to win a men’s professional major in 106 years. He nearly did it — and he took a historic path to finishing just one shot behind McIlroy. Scheffler closed the week going 39 straight holes without a bogey, the longest such streak to finish a Masters in the history of the tournament.

Scottie nearly won despite not taking advantage of two of the historic birdie holes at Augusta National. On the back nine par 5, 13 and 15, Scheffler entered the week with a career score of 23-under par. He played them one-over this week with the lone birdie coming at 15 in the final round.

Scheffler and McIlroy entered the week ranked first and second in the Official World Golf Ranking. This marks the first time the top two players in the ranking finished one-two in a major since Woods won the 2002 U.S. Open with Phil Mickelson finishing runner-up. Scheffler has now finished either first or second in seven of the last 17 men’s major championships contested.

5. It was another heartbreaking Masters Sunday for Justin Rose, who held the outright lead for several holes in the final round. Consecutive bogeys at 11 and 12 derailed Rose’s latest painfully close quest for a green jacket. Rose has now finished in the top three at the Masters four times in his great career. The only player with more Masters top-three finishes who has not won the tournament is Greg Norman (six times).

Rose was excellent with his ball striking all week. He ranked in the top 10 in driving accuracy and top five in both strokes gained tee to green and greens in regulation. But he was just 8-for-17 putting from 5 to 10 feet and ranked 32nd among the 54 players to make the cut in strokes gained on the greens.

Now 45 years old, Rose is the oldest player to finish in the top five in back-to-back years at the same major championship since the 1984 and 1985 PGA Championships, when Lee Trevino won and then finished second the next year. He was the only player in the field to record four rounds under par, the oldest player to do that at the Masters since Kenny Perry (age 48) in 2009.

6. For the third consecutive year, the reigning Players Champion was in the final pairing Sunday at Augusta. Cameron Young couldn’t quite match his two predecessors, though, and a closing 73 left him in a tie for third place. In five Masters starts, Young has accrued three top-10 finishes, this being his best result to date.

Young racked up 11 birdies on the back nine at Augusta through three rounds. He finished his week with nine straight pars Sunday. Per Data Golf, Young lost nearly a stroke and a half to the field on the greens on holes 12 through 16 in the final round.

7. Tyrrell Hatton shot his second 66 of the week Sunday to also finish in a tie for third, his best career result in a major championship. His highlights included a hole out for eagle on the seventh hole, one of two players to earn crystal on the seventh Sunday (fellow Englishman Aaron Rai was the other). He’s finished in the top five now in two of the last three majors played, having recorded a tied-for-fourth result at Oakmont last summer.

8. Russell Henley recorded his best-ever finish in a major championship — a tie for third place — on his 37th birthday, no less. The Georgia native has come into his own in recent years in the game’s biggest events. From 2010 through 2022, Henley failed to register a single top-10 result in any of his 32 major starts. He’s now done so in six of his last 13 tries.

It was a question as to whether Collin Morikawa would even try to tee it up this week as he’s dealing with a back injury. Morikawa did a lot more than that, grinding his way to a fifth consecutive top-15 finish at the Masters. Only Scheffler has an active streak at Augusta that matches Morikawa’s.

9. The top 12 and ties this week will receive tournament invitations in 2027. Notables to earn those spots include Max Homa, whose Sunday 67 vaulted him into a tie for ninth. Homa has just seven top-12 finishes on the PGA Tour in the last three seasons, but three of them have come at the Masters.

Jake Knapp (solo 11th), who led the tournament in strokes gained off the tee, will also get a spot in the 2027 field. In eight starts so far this season, Knapp has finished worse than 11th only once.

10. McIlroy’s win means 11 straight (and 31 of the last 36) Masters winners have come from the final pairing Sunday. Seven of the last nine major champions have ranked either first, second or third entering the week in the OWGR. Before this run, just seven of the previous 29 winners were top three in the OWGR.

The PGA Championship begins in 32 days.
